opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to how people mentally model the prompt. Most folks treat the system prompt as the place where all the "real" instructions live, and the tool definition as API plumbing: a name, a JSON schema, maybe a one-line description. But from the model's point of view, it's all just context. The tool description is text the model reads right at the moment it's deciding whether and how to call that tool. So it's actually one of the most relevant places to put guidance.

When we were building our coding agent for SWE-bench, we spent a surprising amount of time on the tool descriptions rather than on the top-level prompt. For something like a file editing tool, we wrote what was almost a little manual: here's what this tool does, here's when you should use it, here's when you shouldn't, here are the common mistakes. For example, "the old string you're replacing has to match exactly and be unique in the file, so include enough surrounding context." Or "always use absolute paths." That last one came from watching the model wander into a subdirectory and get confused about relative paths. Instead of piling more rules into the system prompt, we just required absolute paths in the tool itself, and that whole class of errors went away.

I think of it as writing documentation for a really smart new hire who's never seen your codebase. If you handed a junior engineer a function with no docstring and a cryptic parameter name, they'd misuse it. People wouldn't do that to a human colleague, but they do it to the model all the time. We sometimes call it "prompt engineering for the agent-computer interface." You should put as much care into the interface the model uses as you would into a UI for people.

The other benefit is that it's modular. If the guidance lives with the tool, it travels with the tool. You can add or remove tools without rewriting a giant system prompt, and each tool's instructions stay local and relevant instead of burying everything in one wall of text the model has to keep in mind.

So my advice is to look at your tool descriptions and ask: if this were the only documentation a capable engineer got, would they use this correctly? If not, that's probably the cheapest improvement available to you.

r001.rationale: The response says the model reads a tool’s description when deciding whether and how to call that tool, making it a relevant place for tool-specific guidance.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think a lot of people, when they think about prompt engineering, they think about the system prompt. That's the big block of text at the top, and that's where all the attention goes. And the tool descriptions are kind of this afterthought where you write one line like "searches the web" or "reads a file" and move on.

But if you actually think about it from the model's perspective, the tool description is the thing it's reading at the exact moment it's deciding whether and how to use that tool. So it's the most contextually relevant place to put guidance about that tool. If I put "always check the file exists before writing to it" way up in the system prompt, that's competing with fifty other instructions, and it's far from the decision point. If I put it in the description of the write tool, the model sees it right when it matters.

The other thing is that tool descriptions are basically free real estate in terms of how models are trained. The model has seen a huge amount of data where a function's docstring tells you how to call it correctly, what the edge cases are, what you shouldn't do. So it's already very good at reading a description and treating that as the authoritative guide for the tool. You're leaning into a prior rather than fighting one.

And honestly, a lot of what we found building Claude Code was that the biggest failure modes were tool-specific. The model would use a bash command when there was a dedicated tool that was safer. Or it would call a search tool with a query that was way too broad. Those are hard to fix with general instructions, because they're really about one tool's behavior. So you put the instruction right there: "Prefer this over running grep in bash," or "Narrow your query before calling this." And it just works, much more reliably than the system prompt version did.

I think the reason it's underutilized is partly that it feels like it shouldn't be prompt engineering. It feels like documentation. But to the model it's all one context window. Everything in there is a prompt, and the description is one of the highest-leverage parts of it because it's so targeted.

r001.rationale: The response says the tool description is read when the model is deciding whether and how to use that tool, making guidance there specifically relevant to that tool.

astra-6.text:
I think people tend to put all the guidance in the system prompt and treat the tool description as just a label—“this function searches the database.” But the tool description is also part of the prompt. It’s a place where you can explain when to use the tool, when not to use it, and what information you need before calling it.

For example, instead of just saying “search,” you can say, “Use this to find documents about a topic. If you already have the document ID, use the fetch tool instead.” Now you’re helping the model make a decision between tools, rather than just describing an API.

And it keeps those instructions attached to the capability they’re about. If you add or remove a tool, the relevant guidance goes with it. It’s a pretty simple thing to try, but I think it gets overlooked because people think of tool definitions as engineering plumbing rather than something they can prompt-engineer.

r001.rationale: The response says the guidance stays attached to the capability it concerns, communicating that the instructions are specifically relevant to that tool.

sol-6.1.text:
I think people tend to treat tool descriptions as API documentation: here’s the function, here are the arguments. But they’re also part of the prompt. They’re a place to tell the model when to use a tool, when not to use it, and what it should do before or after calling it.

For example, if a tool runs a database query, you can put an instruction in its description saying, “Check the schema before writing a query.” That puts the guidance right next to the action it applies to, instead of burying it in a long system prompt.

And it makes things more modular. When you give an agent a tool, the instructions for using that tool come along with it. I think that’s underutilized because we still tend to think of prompting and tool design as separate activities, when really you’re designing one interface for the model.

r001.rationale: The response says the tool description can specify when and how to use that tool, with guidance placed right next to the action it applies to.
